From exact prefix reuse and paged allocation to HBM, host memory, flash, and distributed context storage.

0 · The core problem: preserve useful computation under a memory deadline

A transformer’s KV cache is the materialized history of its causal attention computation. It lets a new token read earlier keys and values without running those earlier tokens through the network again. As contexts, concurrent requests, and repeated agent turns grow, this state competes with model weights for accelerator memory. It also becomes a large recurring read on every decode step and a large transfer when execution moves between devices. The research problem is therefore to minimize the cost of retaining, accessing, and reconstructing useful state while meeting latency and quality constraints.

Three workloads must be separated before comparing methods. An active sequence needs its relevant history at every attention layer of every generated token. A paused sequence needs state when its tool call or user turn returns. A reusable prefix might serve many future requests, but its reuse time and destination are uncertain. HBM, host RAM, flash, and shared storage can all hold KV bytes; that does not mean all can deliver those bytes at the frequency required by active dense attention.

A useful service objective is successful requests per unit cost under a time-to-first-token (TTFT) limit, an inter-token latency (ITL) limit, and a task-quality floor. Optimizing a compression ratio, cache-hit ratio, or kernel latency alone can make this objective worse. A larger host cache may increase hits but create a transfer queue. An aggressive eviction policy may fit more requests but remove the evidence needed for the answer. A long prefix hit can save prefill yet leave decode as expensive as before.

max⁡πE[quality-qualified requests meeting SLOs]costsubject tomemory, bandwidth, and compute capacities,causal cache identity and approximation budget.TTFT=Tqueue+Tlookup/load+Tuncached prefill+Tfirst decode,ITL=Tdecode critical path(including cache transfers).\begin{aligned} \max_{\pi}\quad &\frac{\mathbb E[\text{quality-qualified requests meeting SLOs}]}{\text{cost}}\\ \text{subject to}\quad &\text{memory, bandwidth, and compute capacities},\\ &\text{causal cache identity and approximation budget}.\\[6pt] \mathrm{TTFT}&=T_{\mathrm{queue}}+T_{\mathrm{lookup/load}}\\ &\quad+T_{\mathrm{uncached\ prefill}}+T_{\mathrm{first\ decode}},\\ \mathrm{ITL}&=T_{\mathrm{decode\ critical\ path}}\quad\text{(including cache transfers).} \end{aligned}πmax​subject toTTFTITL​costE[quality-qualified requests meeting SLOs]​memory, bandwidth, and compute capacities,causal cache identity and approximation budget.=Tqueue​+Tlookup/load​+Tuncached prefill​+Tfirst decode​,=Tdecode critical path​(including cache transfers).​

The literature progresses along several interacting branches. Architectural changes reduce how much state exists. Memory managers reduce waste and share valid state. Approximation methods reduce precision or the tokens read. Offloading and distributed systems place state across a hierarchy. Later work increasingly optimizes these choices together because a cache is useful only when it reaches the consuming kernel in time. [1] [4] [14] [19]

1 · Foundations: what exactly is cached?

1.1 Causality makes an unchanged prefix reusable

At layer ℓ and token t, let hℓ,t be the input hidden state and let q, k, v be the projected query, key, and value. Ignoring head indices temporarily, causal attention is:

qℓ,t=WQ,ℓhℓ,t,kℓ,t=WK,ℓhℓ,t,vℓ,t=WV,ℓhℓ,t,sℓ,t,i=qℓ,tTkℓ,id,i≤t,αℓ,t=softmax⁡(sℓ,t,1:t),oℓ,t=∑i≤tαℓ,t,ivℓ,i.\begin{aligned}q_{\ell,t}&=W_{Q,\ell}h_{\ell,t},& k_{\ell,t}&=W_{K,\ell}h_{\ell,t},& v_{\ell,t}&=W_{V,\ell}h_{\ell,t},\\s_{\ell,t,i}&=\frac{q_{\ell,t}^{\mathsf T}k_{\ell,i}}{\sqrt d},&&i\le t,\\\alpha_{\ell,t}&=\operatorname{softmax}(s_{\ell,t,1:t}),\\o_{\ell,t}&=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{\ell,t,i}v_{\ell,i}.\end{aligned}qℓ,t​sℓ,t,i​αℓ,t​oℓ,t​​=WQ,ℓ​hℓ,t​,=d​qℓ,tT​kℓ,i​​,=softmax(sℓ,t,1:t​),=i≤t∑​αℓ,t,i​vℓ,i​.​kℓ,t​=WK,ℓ​hℓ,t​,i≤t,vℓ,t​=WV,ℓ​hℓ,t​,

Positional transformations and attention masks belong in this computation even when omitted from notation. Once token i has been processed, a later appended token cannot change its hidden state under a causal mask. Its K and V can therefore be retained. The query is needed only for the current output calculation and is normally discarded. The cache saves repeated projections and earlier-token layer computation; it does not remove the current query’s interaction with the retained history.

For exact reuse across requests, the prefix must identify the same computation: token IDs, their order and positions, model weights and revision, adapters, positional configuration, attention-mask semantics, and relevant multimodal input state. Equal human-readable strings are insufficient if tokenization or image embeddings differ. Different sampling temperatures after the prefix do not alter an already identical deterministic prefix forward pass, whereas changing an adapter does. Floating-point execution order can introduce small numerical differences even when the mathematical cache is equivalent.

A content hash should include the preceding-prefix identity, not just the current token block. The block containing “the answer is” after document A generally has different deep-layer KV from the same words after document B. This dependency is why prefix caching is straightforward but arbitrary cached-document stitching is an approximation problem. We return to that distinction in CacheBlend. [6] [19] [18]

Derivation: exact prefix reuse follows by induction, not by matching text

Consider two causal-transformer runs with identical token embeddings, positions, model parameters and attention rules through position t. We prove that every layer's hidden states and cached K/V through t are identical in exact arithmetic. The statement concerns deterministic forward computation; stochastic layers or changing external states require the same realized inputs as well.

Base case: at layer zero, corresponding prefix embeddings are equal by assumption. Inductive step: suppose hℓ,i is equal in both runs for every i≤t. For a particular i, causal attention uses only hℓ,1:i. Its queries, keys, values, masked logits and softmax outputs are therefore equal. Residual addition, normalization and the token-local FFN receive equal operands, so hℓ+1,i is equal. Induction over layers proves the cache claim. Appending an arbitrary suffix cannot enter any of these prefix computations through the causal mask.

The same proof fails when the prefix changes before i, when an adapter changes a projection, or when the mask permits future tokens to influence earlier states. Cache identity must encode the computation's dependencies. A token-block hash alone cannot certify equality of the deeper-layer state: equal block text can have unequal ancestors.

Now separate the work saved by caching. Ignoring constants and taking hidden width d, a full prefix of length t costs approximately Atd²+B t²d across fixed-depth layers. Recomputing prefixes for N successive output positions sums this over t, using Σt=Θ(N²) and Σt²=Θ(N³). With KV caching, each new position's projections/FFN cost Ad² and its attention over t history costs B′td, totaling Θ(Nd²+N²d). This explains the large saving while retaining a quadratic total history-read cost over an ever-growing dense sequence. The cache eliminates repeated earlier-token computation, not the new token's need to examine history.

Exercise — Which prefix is reusable?

Two prompts are A‖B‖C and A‖D‖C, where C has exactly the same token IDs and absolute positions. Which regions are guaranteed reusable, and why does C fail the same test?

Show worked solution

A is reusable under the stated identical-model and causal assumptions. C's deep-layer states depend on B in the first run and D in the second, even when C's local token IDs and positions match. Equal positions repair no changed content dependency. In a standard architecture, some earliest-layer projections may be identical for C before contextual attention, but that does not validate the full multilayer KV cache.

1.2 MHA → MQA → GQA: fewer KV heads

In multi-head attention (MHA), each query head has its own K and V head. Multi-query attention (MQA, 2019) retains many query heads but shares one K/V head among them. Grouped-query attention (GQA, 2023) uses an intermediate number of KV heads. For Hq query heads and Hkv KV heads, the group size is Hq/Hkv when the division is uniform. Query expressiveness is partly retained while KV storage and reads fall with Hkv. GQA’s paper also describes uptraining an existing MHA checkpoint after pooling key/value head weights, avoiding the need to train every architecture from scratch. [1] [2]

The benefit is architectural rather than a runtime lossless compression of an arbitrary MHA model. Changing head sharing changes the network. Nor does the storage ratio guarantee an equal speedup: projections, FFNs, output heads, and communication remain. A kernel that expands shared KV into per-query-head buffers can squander the memory advantage. Head-wise eviction must also respect sharing; allocating independent token subsets to query heads can require the union of those subsets for their shared KV head.

1.3 MLA: cache the latent, then absorb projections

DeepSeek-V2’s multi-head latent attention (MLA) changes the stored representation more substantially. It compresses a token’s content KV into cᵢ of dimension dc and uses learned up-projections to recover per-head keys and values. A separate positional key component handles rotary embedding. In the content-only algebra:

ki,h=UK,hci,vi,h=UV,hci,qt,hTki,h=(UK,hTqt,h)Tci,∑iαt,i,hvi,h=UV,h ⁣(∑iαt,i,hci).Conventional scalars/token/layer=Hkv(dK+dV),MLA scalars/token/layer≈dc+dR.\begin{aligned}k_{i,h}&=U_{K,h}c_i,&v_{i,h}&=U_{V,h}c_i,\\q_{t,h}^{\mathsf T}k_{i,h}&=(U_{K,h}^{\mathsf T}q_{t,h})^{\mathsf T}c_i,\\\sum_i\alpha_{t,i,h}v_{i,h}&=U_{V,h}\!\left(\sum_i\alpha_{t,i,h}c_i\right).\\[6pt]\text{Conventional scalars/token/layer}&=H_{\mathrm{kv}}(d_K+d_V),\\\text{MLA scalars/token/layer}&\approx d_c+d_R.\end{aligned}ki,h​qt,hT​ki,h​i∑​αt,i,h​vi,h​Conventional scalars/token/layerMLA scalars/token/layer​=UK,h​ci​,=(UK,hT​qt,h​)Tci​,=UV,h​(i∑​αt,i,h​ci​).=Hkv​(dK​+dV​),≈dc​+dR​.​vi,h​=UV,h​ci​,

The second line moves the key up-projection onto the query and the value up-projection after the weighted latent sum. This makes storing the expanded per-head tensors unnecessary during the corresponding decode computation. Position-dependent rotations cannot generally be absorbed into a fixed matrix in the same way; MLA’s decoupled positional branch addresses that obstruction. Count the actual latent and positional tensors, including any replicated copies, instead of pretending MLA is GQA with a fractional number of heads. Prefill and decode may use different kernel representations, so conversion/workspace can matter at phase boundaries. [3]

Derivation: latent KV absorption works only across compatible operators

Use column vectors. A content key and value are kᵢ=Uₖcᵢ and vᵢ=Uᵥcᵢ, with latent cᵢ∈ℝ^r and expanded width d. For query q, associativity gives qᵀUₖcᵢ=(Uₖᵀq)ᵀcᵢ. The query can be projected into latent space once; each historical cᵢ stays compressed. Linearity gives ΣᵢαᵢUᵥcᵢ=UᵥΣᵢαᵢcᵢ, so the value expansion can follow the weighted sum. These moves are exact because the moved matrices do not depend on i.

Now insert positional rotations Rₜ and Rᵢ into queries and keys:

(Rtq)T(RiUkci)=qTRtTRiUkci=(UkTRiTRtq)Tci.\begin{aligned}(R_tq)^{\mathsf T}(R_iU_kc_i)&=q^{\mathsf T}R_t^{\mathsf T}R_iU_kc_i\\&=(U_k^{\mathsf T}R_i^{\mathsf T}R_tq)^{\mathsf T}c_i.\end{aligned}(Rt​q)T(Ri​Uk​ci​)​=qTRtT​Ri​Uk​ci​=(UkT​RiT​Rt​q)Tci​.​

The proposed latent query now depends on historical position i. Computing one shared transformed query for all i is generally impossible. A sufficient special condition would be a family of latent rotations Tᵢ satisfying RᵢUₖ=UₖTᵢ together with a compatible implementation; an arbitrary learned Uₖ does not ensure it. Simply deleting Rᵢ or commuting it through Uₖ changes logits.

This is the obstruction addressed by separating content and positional components in MLA. If q=(qC,qR) and k=(Uₖc,kR), then qᵀk=(UₖᵀqC)ᵀc+qRᵀkR. Store c and the positional component kR, expand the content query once, and compute the positional term separately. The cache saves dimensions when r+dR is smaller than the expanded content K/V total; the additional operations and head-dependent attention still need kernels. A smaller latent is an architectural bottleneck learned with the model, not a lossless compression available for every pretrained MHA checkpoint.

1.4 Bytes, pages, metadata, and the batch crossover

For sequence b of length Sb, layer ℓ with Hkv,ℓ heads, widths dK,ℓ and dV,ℓ, and payload bit widths βK,ℓ and βV,ℓ:

Mpayload=18∑b∑ℓSbHkv,ℓ(dK,ℓβK,ℓ+dV,ℓβV,ℓ),MBF16=2BSLHkvd×2  bytes.N scalars; G values/group; s scale bits; z zero-point bits:Mencoded,bits=Nβ+⌈NG⌉(s+z)+Boutlier,bits+Bpadding,bits,βeffective=Mencoded,bitsN.Nallocated=∑bP⌈SbP⌉,Mdevice=Mweights+Mencoded KV+Mpage metadata+Mworkspace+Mcommunication+Mallocator/runtime.\begin{aligned} M_{\mathrm{payload}}&=\frac18\sum_b\sum_\ell S_bH_{\mathrm{kv},\ell}\bigl(d_{K,\ell}\beta_{K,\ell}+d_{V,\ell}\beta_{V,\ell}\bigr),\\ M_{\mathrm{BF16}}&=2BSLH_{\mathrm{kv}}d\times2\;\mathrm{bytes}.\\[8pt] &\text{$N$ scalars; $G$ values/group; $s$ scale bits; $z$ zero-point bits:}\\ M_{\mathrm{encoded,bits}}&=N\beta+\left\lceil\frac NG\right\rceil(s+z)\\ &\quad+B_{\mathrm{outlier,bits}}+B_{\mathrm{padding,bits}},\\ \beta_{\mathrm{effective}}&=\frac{M_{\mathrm{encoded,bits}}}{N}.\\[8pt] N_{\mathrm{allocated}}&=\sum_bP\left\lceil\frac{S_b}{P}\right\rceil,\\ M_{\mathrm{device}}&=M_{\mathrm{weights}}+M_{\mathrm{encoded\ KV}}+M_{\mathrm{page\ metadata}}\\ &\quad+M_{\mathrm{workspace}}+M_{\mathrm{communication}}\\ &\quad+M_{\mathrm{allocator/runtime}}. \end{aligned}Mpayload​MBF16​Mencoded,bits​βeffective​Nallocated​Mdevice​​=81​b∑​ℓ∑​Sb​Hkv,ℓ​(dK,ℓ​βK,ℓ​+dV,ℓ​βV,ℓ​),=2BSLHkv​d×2bytes.N scalars; G values/group; s scale bits; z zero-point bits:=Nβ+⌈GN​⌉(s+z)+Boutlier,bits​+Bpadding,bits​,=NMencoded,bits​​.=b∑​P⌈PSb​​⌉,=Mweights​+Mencoded KV​+Mpage metadata​+Mworkspace​+Mcommunication​+Mallocator/runtime​.​

With L=32, Hkv=8, d=128 and BF16, each token requires 128 KiB across layers. One 131,072-token sequence therefore uses 16 GiB of payload. Eight use 128 GiB. This is already larger than many single-device memory capacities before weights are included. A 16-bit scale per 128 eight-bit values yields 8 + 16/128 = 8.125 bits/value, before tails or alignment. Effective bits are a ratio over a specified population; dividing total model memory by KV scalar count would mix unrelated costs.

Uniform conventional K/V representation. MLA, mixed layers, per-group metadata, and tensor-parallel replication need a different count.

Tensor parallelism does not automatically divide this memory by its degree. KV heads can be replicated when the number of ranks exceeds the available independent heads, and some latent implementations replicate their cache. With prefix sharing, the sequence sum should count each unique physical block once, plus private suffixes. A full layer cache and a sliding-window layer cache also have different Sb. These details routinely change capacity estimates by multiples.

For a simple decode layer, reading K and V costs approximately 2SHkv d·w bytes per sequence, while the two attention matrix-vector products cost about 4SHq d FLOPs. The resulting idealized arithmetic intensity is 2(Hq/Hkv)/w FLOPs/byte, assuming shared KV is effectively reused among its query heads. It does not grow with S. Longer contexts enlarge the stream rather than creating weight-like batch reuse. Across independent sequences, model weights can be reused in a batch but their KV generally cannot. Consequently, increasing batch size often shifts the bottleneck from weight traffic toward KV traffic. This is the architectural reason cache management remains important even on accelerators with very fast matrix units.

2 · 2023–2025: allocation becomes a virtual-memory problem

2.1 PagedAttention: allocate the history that exists

Earlier serving systems often reserved a contiguous maximum-length region for each sequence. Three losses followed: unused space reserved for future output, internal slack inside assigned regions, and external holes that could not accommodate a large request. PagedAttention, introduced with vLLM in 2023, represents each sequence as fixed-size logical token blocks mapped to physical blocks allocated as needed. Token order stays logical; physical order can be arbitrary. [4]

Reading the figure. The yellow request and green request occupy different reserved extents. Most of the apparently unavailable memory is not storing useful tokens. A capacity gain comes from admitting more concurrent work into those freed bytes, not from reducing the mathematical number of K/V scalars per live token. This distinction explains why reported serving throughput gains depend strongly on length distributions and the previous allocator.

The attention kernel loads the block-table entry, computes the physical address, and gathers the appropriate K/V tiles. It must maintain one correct softmax normalization over the logical history. Computing independent block outputs and simply averaging them is wrong. If block j has local maximum mj, exponential sum lj, and normalized weighted output oj, two blocks combine through a numerically stable merge:

m=max⁡(m1,m2),l=em1−ml1+em2−ml2,o=em1−ml1o1+em2−ml2o2l.\begin{aligned}m&=\max(m_1,m_2),\\l&=e^{m_1-m}l_1+e^{m_2-m}l_2,\\o&=\frac{e^{m_1-m}l_1o_1+e^{m_2-m}l_2o_2}{l}.\end{aligned}mlo​=max(m1​,m2​),=em1​−ml1​+em2​−ml2​,=lem1​−ml1​o1​+em2​−ml2​o2​​.​

This associative reduction, up to floating-point ordering, also supports partitioned attention kernels. Paging is an address-management choice; tiling and softmax reduction determine how efficiently the kernel executes it. Block size trades tail waste against indexing, locality, scheduling, and transport overhead. The paper’s token-block size is not a hardware memory-page size.

Derivation: exact attention across independently stored pages

Let page j contain logits sᵢ and values vᵢ. Store three sufficient statistics for its contribution: mⱼ=maxᵢsᵢ, lⱼ=Σᵢexp(sᵢ−mⱼ), and uⱼ=Σᵢexp(sᵢ−mⱼ)vᵢ. Here u is unnormalized. Its locally normalized output is oⱼ=uⱼ/lⱼ. A page output alone loses its total probability mass and cannot be averaged with other pages correctly.

For two pages choose m=max(m₁,m₂). Multiplying a page's stored sum by exp(mⱼ−m) changes its reference exponent but not its mathematical contribution:

∑i∈page jesi−m=emj−mlj,∑i∈page jesi−mvi=emj−muj,l=em1−ml1+em2−ml2,u=em1−mu1+em2−mu2,o=ul.\begin{aligned}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{page}\ j}e^{s_i-m}&=e^{m_j-m}l_j,\\\sum_{i\in\mathrm{page}\ j}e^{s_i-m}v_i&=e^{m_j-m}u_j,\\l&=e^{m_1-m}l_1+e^{m_2-m}l_2,\\u&=e^{m_1-m}u_1+e^{m_2-m}u_2,\\o&=\frac ul.\end{aligned}i∈page j∑​esi​−mi∈page j∑​esi​−mvi​luo​=emj​−mlj​,=emj​−muj​,=em1​−ml1​+em2​−ml2​,=em1​−mu1​+em2​−mu2​,=lu​.​

The merged pair again represents the same two sums over the union. Merging a third page therefore preserves the invariant, proving by induction that block order and reduction-tree shape do not change exact real-number attention. Floating-point rounding can differ with order. Empty pages require an explicit empty-state convention, avoiding undefined expressions such as −∞−(−∞).

This derivation connects paging, FlashAttention-style online softmax, split-K decode and distributed attention. They differ in where blocks reside and how partial statistics move. Their exactness comes from preserving the same sums, not from contiguous storage or a particular kernel name. It also explains why exchanging a small output vector and normalization statistics can replace gathering all value vectors after distributed local attention.

Exercise — Why averaging page outputs is wrong

Page A contains logits (0,0) and values (0,2). Page B contains one logit log(2) and value 4. Compute the correct merged result and the result from averaging the two page means.

Show worked solution

Page A has mA=0, lA=2, uA=2 and oA=1. Page B has mB=log2, lB=1, uB=4 and oB=4. Rescaling to m=log2 gives l=0.5·2+1=2 and u=0.5·2+4=5, hence o=2.5. Averaging local outputs also happens to give (1+4)/2=2.5 here because both pages have equal unnormalized mass. This is a deliberate diagnostic: the shortcut can pass a toy test accidentally. Change B's logit to log4; now the correct output is (2+16)/(2+4)=3, while the unweighted page average remains 2.5. A good correctness test varies page mass independently of page count.

2.2 Sharing, branching, and the last partial block

Shared prefix blocks can be referenced by several sequences. Reference counts prevent reclamation while a live user remains. Complete immutable blocks are easy to share; appending into a shared partially filled block requires copy-on-write. Only the diverging writable block needs a new physical copy, while earlier blocks remain shared. Beam search, parallel sampling, and repeated prompts can therefore avoid duplicating large prefixes. [4]

In the original example, both samples refer to physical block 7 for their first four tokens. The next block contains the divergence. One sample obtains a copied block before replacing the continuation, and the reference count on the old block falls. This is a correctness mechanism as well as a memory optimization: in-place modification of a shared prefix would corrupt another request.

Admission still needs a future-growth policy. A batch can fit at its current length and fail after many more decode steps. Reserving all possible future pages wastes capacity; reserving none requires a preemption strategy. Swapping, recomputation, delayed admission, and output-length estimates have different tail-latency and fairness consequences. A useful trace should record preemptions and wasted recompute, not only average page utilization.

2.3 vAttention: move the mapping below the kernel

vAttention’s 2024 preprint, published at ASPLOS 2025, keeps a contiguous virtual KV address range and maps physical GPU pages into it incrementally. Existing attention kernels can see a contiguous tensor while physical backing remains dynamic. The contribution is an alternative location for indirection, plus techniques to make allocation and mapping keep up with token generation. Virtual address reservation is not physical memory reservation. [5]

Panels (a)–(e) show an initially unbacked range, allocation for R1, growth plus R2, reclamation when R1 exits, and arrival of R3. The physical pages need not follow the visible virtual sequence. This reduces the need to rewrite every attention kernel around software block tables. It does not eliminate physical-page granularity, mapping costs, or the need to schedule allocation before a kernel touches a page.

The appropriate comparison is the complete allocator–kernel pair. A faster nonpaged FlashAttention kernel can make vAttention attractive; a highly optimized paged kernel can narrow the gap. GPU virtual-memory APIs, driver behavior, supported page sizes, and amortized mapping frequency affect portability. Neither design makes prefix sharing or eviction policy automatic. Both need explicit lifetime management above the address translation layer.

3 · Prefix locality becomes a scheduling resource

3.1 SGLang / RadixAttention: retain the branching computation

SGLang’s RadixAttention stores token-prefix paths in a radix tree. A compressed edge represents a run of tokens rather than one node per token. A request walks the tree to find its longest cached prefix; if it diverges inside an edge, the edge is split at the common prefix. Newly computed suffix KV is inserted when appropriate. The tree tracks references so active requests protect the state they use, while an LRU policy can reclaim eligible leaves. [6]

Follow the nine states. Early chat turns share the system prompt and conversation history. A divergent user request creates a branch. Few-shot examples create another reusable path. Later parallel continuations fan out below shared nodes. Evicting a leaf can expose its parent as a new candidate; evicting an internal ancestor while live descendants depend on it would invalidate their prefix. The actual cached object is the executed token path, not an application-level chat label.

Cache-aware scheduling can process requests with related prefixes together, reducing repeated eviction and loading. SGLang analyzes a tree traversal scheduling view in which grouping related work improves reuse under a finite cache. However, a perfect offline traversal assumes knowledge and freedom that an online latency-sensitive service may not have. Arrivals, priorities, and decode deadlines limit how long a request can wait for a cache-friendly order.

3.2 Preble: locality competes with load balance

Preble extends prefix-aware scheduling across workers. A request can go to the worker with the longest matching prefix, the shortest queue, or a compromise. Always maximizing local hits can overload the worker that holds a popular system prompt. Always selecting the emptiest worker can repeatedly recompute expensive prefixes. Distributed scheduling therefore needs an estimate of saved prefill work together with queued computation and movement cost. [7]

A simple analytical dispatch rule illustrates the tradeoff without claiming to reproduce any one implementation:

T^finish(w)=Tqueue(w)+min⁡ ⁣{Tload(cached prefix at w),  Trecompute(prefix)}+Tuncached suffix(w),w∗=arg min⁡w meeting capacity/SLO constraintsT^finish(w).\begin{aligned}\widehat T_{\mathrm{finish}}(w)&=T_{\mathrm{queue}}(w)\\&\quad+\min\!\left\{T_{\mathrm{load}}(\text{cached prefix at }w),\;T_{\mathrm{recompute}}(\text{prefix})\right\}\\&\quad+T_{\mathrm{uncached\ suffix}}(w),\\w^*&=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{w\,\text{meeting capacity/SLO constraints}}\widehat T_{\mathrm{finish}}(w).\end{aligned}Tfinish​(w)w∗​=Tqueue​(w)+min{Tload​(cached prefix at w),Trecompute​(prefix)}+Tuncached suffix​(w),=wmeeting capacity/SLO constraintsargmin​Tfinish​(w).​

If a local hit saves 120 ms but its worker has 400 ms more queued work, locality alone is the wrong decision. If the prefix is 100K tokens and the queue difference is 20 ms, recomputation can dominate. Replicating very popular prefixes can be profitable, but consumes capacity that might retain many less frequent ones. A global index should distinguish availability from readiness: a block being written, evicted, or transferred is not necessarily an immediately usable hit.

3.3 Prefix organization is part of application performance

Place stable shared material early when prompt semantics permit it: a common system instruction before per-request content creates reusable paths. A unique timestamp at the beginning can invalidate all later exact-prefix reuse. This is a consequence of causal identity, not a request to alter the task’s meaning for cache hits. Structured agents with long tool pauses also benefit from explicit lifetime hints when an engine supports them; otherwise the cache manager must infer whether a conversation will return.

The best reuse metric is not merely requests with a hit. Measure matched tokens, avoided prefill time, bytes retained, residence time, and actual TTFT saved. Reusing 20 tokens and reusing 20,000 tokens count equally in a binary hit rate but have very different economic value. Hash/index overhead can dominate tiny prefixes, whereas transfer bandwidth can dominate very large ones.

4 · 2023–2025: which historical tokens deserve memory?

4.1 H2O: online heavy hitters and irreversible eviction

H2O accumulates attention evidence to identify historically important tokens, keeping these heavy hitters alongside a recent-token window. Recency provides continuity and gives new tokens an opportunity to become important; accumulated scores protect older tokens that repeatedly attract attention. Under a fixed budget, a low-value candidate is evicted as new state arrives. This is an online retention policy: once a token is removed from the only copy, a later query cannot recover it without recomputation. [10]

A conceptual score is a cumulative sum aᵢ(t)=Στ≤t ατ,i, with the exact update restricted to what the policy observes and retains. The historical statistic is predictive only when future attention resembles its past. A document identifier ignored for hundreds of tokens can become crucial when a later question asks about it. Theoretical results in H2O use assumptions about a dynamic submodular objective; they are not a universal guarantee of unchanged transformer outputs for arbitrary prompts.

Dense attention-score instrumentation also has a cost. Modern fused attention avoids materializing the full attention matrix. An eviction method that needs a large score tensor can reintroduce traffic or require a specialized score reduction. Its measured memory saving must include this temporary workspace and any retained score metadata.

4.2 StreamingLLM: attention sinks stabilize a finite window

StreamingLLM observes that initial tokens can receive substantial attention even when semantically unimportant. Softmax must distribute probability somewhere, and these tokens can become sinks. Dropping them abruptly while retaining only recent tokens destabilizes generation. Keeping a few initial sink tokens plus a rolling recent window restores stable streaming perplexity in the studied models. [11]

Read the two distinct claims in the figure. A rolling cache bounds storage and per-step work. Preserving sink tokens improves behavior compared with naively discarding the beginning. Neither claim says a four-million-token stream remains fully retrievable from a tiny cache. Old content outside the retained set is gone. Streaming is processing an indefinitely long sequence with bounded state; full long-context recall is a different capability.

Position handling also matters. The paper’s implementation assigns positions consistently with its rolling-cache scheme rather than simply leaving ever-growing absolute RoPE indices on a truncated window. Copying only the sink policy while changing its positional convention can produce different results. A practical test must include information whose answer depends on distant evicted content, not only next-token perplexity dominated by recent context.

4.3 SnapKV: use the question-bearing prompt suffix as evidence

SnapKV compresses prompt KV before generation. An observation window near the end of the prompt attends over earlier positions. For each head, attention from these queries is aggregated into a score for previous tokens. Pooling spreads importance to neighboring positions so a selected semantic span is less likely to lose supporting words. The highest-scoring earlier positions are retained along with the observation window. [12]

The green suffix in the figure contains the question; its attention votes identify orange regions in the earlier document. Selection is head-specific because different heads use different evidence. Pooling is more than a cosmetic smoothing step: if attention spikes on one token inside an entity, nearby tokens may contain the rest of the entity or its relation. A pure isolated top-k can keep the anchor and discard the context that makes it useful.

This is an empirical prediction about future generation. The observation window already knows the initial question, making the setting question-aware. A reusable cache compressed before any future question is known has less information. Reusing the same aggressively compressed document for unrelated later questions can fail even if the original one-turn benchmark is strong. Long generated reasoning may also create new information needs absent from the last prompt window. Distinguish compression of the prompt from any separate policy for subsequently generated tokens.

4.4 PyramidKV, Ada-KV, HeadKV: allocate budget where it matters

PyramidKV observes an information-funneling pattern across depth: lower layers often spread attention over more content, while higher layers show greater concentration. It gives larger budgets to lower layers and smaller budgets to upper layers while retaining an overall budget. Within a layer, its selection builds on observation-window importance. The important change is allocation across layers, not a new universal token-importance oracle. [13]

The six heatmaps are evidence for the model/prompt in the paper. A layer number is not a fixed semantic role shared by every architecture. A different model, task, or reasoning phase can change the distribution. A pyramidal allocation should therefore be evaluated against a uniform budget at the same total bytes, including different head counts and metadata, rather than at the same nominal maximum tokens in just one layer.

Ada-KV goes a level finer, allocating budgets across heads. For a fixed set of observed attention weights, concatenate the heads’ scores, select the largest B entries globally, and count how many came from each head. These counts define the individual budgets. Concentrated heads need relatively few entries to retain most probability mass; diffuse heads receive more. The method plugs into SnapKV or PyramidKV and adds a minimum allocation safeguard. Its analysis minimizes an upper bound on eviction loss, not the actual future task loss. [27]

A simple related bound makes the objective intuitive. Let S be the retained set for one head, r=Σi∈S αi its original attention mass, and assume every value vector has norm at most Vmax. Renormalizing attention over S gives oS. Then:

o=r oS+(1−r)ooutside,∥o−oS∥≤(1−r)(∥oS∥+∥ooutside∥)≤2Vmax⁡(1−r).\begin{aligned}o&=r\,o_S+(1-r)o_{\mathrm{outside}},\\\lVert o-o_S\rVert&\le(1-r)(\lVert o_S\rVert+\lVert o_{\mathrm{outside}}\rVert)\\&\le2V_{\max}(1-r).\end{aligned}o∥o−oS​∥​=roS​+(1−r)ooutside​,≤(1−r)(∥oS​∥+∥ooutside​∥)≤2Vmax​(1−r).​

This derivation concerns the current fixed q, K, V and a norm bound; it does not establish the same bound after approximation errors propagate through later layers and tokens. It nevertheless explains why retaining attention mass is a useful surrogate. Ada-KV’s full multi-head analysis incorporates output-projection/value bounds. Efficient GQA support requires aggregating decisions at shared KV groups; otherwise per-query-head copies can quietly erase GQA’s storage savings.

HeadKV uses a different source of evidence: head-importance profiling for retrieval and contextual reasoning. HeadKV-R estimates retrieval ability, while HeadKV-R2 broadens the probe toward reasoning-relevant information. Budgets combine a baseline allocation with an importance-weighted component. This differs from Ada-KV’s per-input concentration allocation: a head can be sharply focused yet play a crucial task role. The two criteria answer different questions—how dispersed is attention now, and which heads tend to perform useful operations? Their estimates can shift with domain and task. [28]

4.5 Quest: read fewer tokens without deleting the full history

Quest keeps the full cache and stores coordinate-wise minimum and maximum keys for each page. Given the current query, these summaries estimate which pages could contain high dot products. Let mj,c and Mj,c be the minimum and maximum coordinate c in page j. Then for every key k in that page:

qTk≤Uj(q)=∑cmax⁡(qcmj,c,qcMj,c)=∑qc≥0qcMj,c+∑qc<0qcmj,c.\begin{aligned}q^{\mathsf T}k\le U_j(q)&=\sum_c\max(q_cm_{j,c},q_cM_{j,c})\\&=\sum_{q_c\ge0}q_cM_{j,c}+\sum_{q_c<0}q_cm_{j,c}.\end{aligned}qTk≤Uj​(q)​=c∑​max(qc​mj,c​,qc​Mj,c​)=qc​≥0∑​qc​Mj,c​+qc​<0∑​qc​mj,c​.​

A page score therefore costs a scan over compact min/max metadata instead of all its keys. Quest ranks pages, reads the selected ones, and computes attention on that subset. Positive query coordinates prefer maxima; negative ones prefer minima. The maximizing coordinate values may come from different tokens, so Uj can be loose. Selecting the pages with the highest bounds is a heuristic for useful attention mass, not a proof that every omitted page contributes zero. [14]

In the figure, stage 1 uses only the summaries and query. Stage 2 loads the chosen page contents. For page size P, min/max key metadata uses roughly 2/P of the key payload’s scalar count, assuming the same precision and widths. Against both K and V payload together, its relative fraction is smaller. Larger pages reduce summary cost but make the bound looser and fetch more irrelevant tokens; smaller pages improve selectivity but increase scoring and top-k overhead.

The full KV remains available for a later query that suddenly asks about old content. Thus Quest primarily saves HBM read bandwidth and attention work, not total full-cache capacity. It can be combined with offloading, but then page residency and transfers become additional design problems. Its implementation also treats early layers conservatively where attention is less sparse. This is why “keep 2048 tokens” means something materially different for Quest and for permanent eviction.

For Llama2-7B at 32K context and a 2048-token budget, the paper reports 7.03× attention speedup over FlashInfer on RTX 4090; its end-to-end Ada 6000 evaluation gives gains of 1.74× with FP16 weights and 2.23× with four-bit weights. The displayed arrow at 32K instead marks the 4096-token row, giving 4.86×. Weight quantization increases attention’s share of the remaining runtime, so the same attention optimization produces a larger total gain. This is an instructive bottleneck shift rather than a contradiction between the numbers. [14]

Derivation: page bounds can certify an omitted-mass error budget

Quest uses page scores for selection. The following is a mathematical consequence of valid page upper bounds, not a claim that Quest's published implementation supplies this certificate. Suppose page j has nj tokens and Uj≥maxᵢ∈j sᵢ for the actual scaled attention logits s=qᵀk/√d. Coordinatewise extrema give such an upper bound because each term qc kc is bounded by the larger endpoint product; summing preserves the inequality.

Let S be the selected pages and compute their exact partition sum ZS=Σᵢ∈S exp(sᵢ). For omitted pages, each exponential is at most exp(Uj), so:

ZE=∑i∉Sesi≤R=∑j∉SnjeUj,ε=ZEZS+ZE≤RZS+R.\begin{aligned}Z_E&=\sum_{i\notin S}e^{s_i}\le R=\sum_{j\notin S}n_je^{U_j},\\\varepsilon&=\frac{Z_E}{Z_S+Z_E}\le\frac{R}{Z_S+R}.\end{aligned}ZE​ε​=i∈/S∑​esi​≤R=j∈/S∑​nj​eUj​,=ZS​+ZE​ZE​​≤ZS​+RR​.​

The second inequality holds because x/(ZS+x) increases with x for positive ZS. In a numerically stable implementation all sums can use one common maximum offset; the ratio is unchanged.

Let oS and oE be normalized attention outputs on selected and omitted tokens. Full attention obeys o=(1−ε)oS+εoE. If every value has norm at most Vmax, convexity gives ∥oS∥,∥oE∥≤Vmax. Therefore:

∥o−oS∥=ε∥oE−oS∥≤2Vmax⁡ε≤2Vmax⁡RZS+R.\begin{aligned}\lVert o-o_S\rVert&=\varepsilon\lVert o_E-o_S\rVert\le2V_{\max}\varepsilon\\&\le\frac{2V_{\max}R}{Z_S+R}.\end{aligned}∥o−oS​∥​=ε∥oE​−oS​∥≤2Vmax​ε≤ZS​+R2Vmax​R​.​

To enforce output error at most η<2Vmax, it suffices to reduce R until R≤η ZS/(2Vmax−η). Bounds can be very loose because different coordinate extrema may belong to different keys, and summing nj upper-bound exponentials assumes every omitted token reaches its page bound. Tight certificates may require reading most pages. This separates a guarantee under an explicit norm bound from an empirically effective top-page heuristic.

Exercise — Turn a logit bound into an output guarantee

Selected pages have ZS=90, while omitted-page bounds give R=10. If every value norm is at most 3, bound the output error. What R suffices for an error target of 0.2 at the same ZS?

Show worked solution

ε≤10/(90+10)=0.1, hence ∥o−oS∥≤2·3·0.1=0.6. For η=0.2, require R≤0.2·90/(6−0.2)=18/5.8≈3.10345. This is sufficient, not necessary: cancellations among omitted value vectors can make the true error much smaller.

5 · 2024–2026: quantize the state that attention actually uses

5.1 Error in keys and error in values have different effects

Let the reconstructed tensors be K+ΔK and V+ΔV. Key error perturbs logits before a nonlinear normalization; value error perturbs the weighted output after normalization. A first-order expansion for one query is:

δs=qTΔKd,δα≈[diag⁡(α)−ααT]δs,δo≈∑iδαi vi+∑iαi δvi.\begin{aligned}\delta s&=\frac{q^{\mathsf T}\Delta K}{\sqrt d},\\\delta\alpha&\approx\bigl[\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)-\alpha\alpha^{\mathsf T}\bigr]\delta s,\\\delta o&\approx\sum_i\delta\alpha_i\,v_i+\sum_i\alpha_i\,\delta v_i.\end{aligned}δsδαδo​=d​qTΔK​,≈[diag(α)−ααT]δs,≈i∑​δαi​vi​+i∑​αi​δvi​.​

The first term can redirect attention among tokens; the second is weighted by the original attention distribution. Minimizing raw tensor reconstruction error alone need not minimize output error. A small error on the value of a highly attended token can matter more than a large error on thousands of irrelevant tokens. Likewise, a coherent key error aligned with the query can matter more than a larger error in an orthogonal direction. This is why keys and values often need different quantization axes, formats, or protection rules. [15] [16]

Derivation: a key-error budget becomes a probability and output-error budget

Assume one fixed query q, original keys ki and reconstructed keys ki+δki with ∥δki∥₂≤εK. Cauchy–Schwarz gives a uniform logit perturbation bound εs=∥q∥₂ εK/√d. Let pi=exp(si)/Z and p̂i=exp(si+δsi)/Ẑ. Since every δsi lies in [−εs,εs], summing exponential inequalities gives exp(−εs)Z≤Ẑ≤exp(εs)Z.

p^ipi=eδsiZZ^∈[e−2εs,e2εs],∑i∣p^i−pi∣≤e2εs−1,∑i∣p^i−pi∣≤2(independently).\begin{aligned}\frac{\widehat p_i}{p_i}&=e^{\delta s_i}\frac Z{\widehat Z}\in[e^{-2\varepsilon_s},e^{2\varepsilon_s}],\\\sum_i|\widehat p_i-p_i|&\le e^{2\varepsilon_s}-1,\\\sum_i|\widehat p_i-p_i|&\le2\qquad\text{(independently).}\end{aligned}pi​p​i​​i∑​∣p​i​−pi​∣i∑​∣p​i​−pi​∣​=eδsi​ZZ​∈[e−2εs​,e2εs​],≤e2εs​−1,≤2(independently).​

The first L1 bound follows by bounding each |p̂i/pi−1| by exp(2εs)−1 and summing pi=1. It is conservative but finite, unlike a first-order Taylor approximation. If original values satisfy ∥vi∥≤Vmax and each value error has norm at most εV:

o^−o=∑i(p^i−pi)vi+∑ip^i δvi,∥o^−o∥≤Vmax⁡min⁡ ⁣(2,e2εs−1)+εV.\begin{aligned}\widehat o-o&=\sum_i(\widehat p_i-p_i)v_i+\sum_i\widehat p_i\,\delta v_i,\\\lVert\widehat o-o\rVert&\le V_{\max}\min\!\left(2,e^{2\varepsilon_s}-1\right)+\varepsilon_V.\end{aligned}o−o∥o−o∥​=i∑​(p​i​−pi​)vi​+i∑​p​i​δvi​,≤Vmax​min(2,e2εs​−1)+εV​.​

The key term depends on query norm and softmax redistribution; the direct value term averages errors with probabilities summing to one. This provides a rigorous reason to distinguish K and V precision, but does not prove keys always deserve more bits. Actual directions, attention concentration and model amplification matter. The bound assumes the same query and upstream states; after many quantized layers, q itself changes and must be included in a full perturbation analysis.

The first-order Jacobian formula in the main text is recovered from differentiating log pi=si−logΣjexp(sj): δpi=pi(δsi−Σjpjδsj). A common shift δsi=c cancels exactly. An error metric that penalizes this common shift as if it redirected attention is overly pessimistic. This helps explain why raw key reconstruction MSE is only a proxy for task-relevant error.

Exercise — A large logit error that changes nothing

Original logits are (2,0,−1). A quantized path returns (12,10,9). What happens to attention probabilities? Why can a norm-based error bound look poor anyway?

Show worked solution

All three logits increased by 10. Factoring exp(10) from numerator and denominator shows softmax(s+10·1)=softmax(s), exactly in real arithmetic. A worst-case bound using εs=10 ignores the shared direction and becomes vacuous after clipping at L1≤2. This is not a contradiction: an upper bound covers adversarial nonuniform perturbations as well as benign common shifts.

5.2 KIVI: asymmetric grouping plus a residual window

KIVI finds persistent high-magnitude channels in keys. Per-token quantization makes a large channel set the range for many ordinary channels in the same token. Per-channel quantization instead groups values of one channel across tokens, isolating that channel’s scale. Values have a less persistent channel-outlier pattern, and per-token grouping better confines errors to individual tokens before the sparse attention-weighted sum. The paper explicitly compares attention-output error, not just the shape of the activation histogram. [15]

The plots show why the key axis matters. In the Llama-2-13B example, large values recur along particular channels over many tokens. The value plots do not show the same stable ridges. KIVI’s Table 2 is especially instructive: a value quantizer can have a smaller raw reconstruction error and still have a much larger weighted attention-output error. Optimizing the consumer of a tensor can change the preferred grouping.

The streaming difficulty is that a key group spans tokens that have not all arrived yet. KIVI keeps a recent full-precision residual region and converts completed groups into low-bit form. The old quantized region and recent high-precision region are both used in attention. The implementation fuses dequantization with tiled multiplication to avoid writing a fully expanded historical cache to HBM. [15]

A low-bit label must include the residual’s cost. For S tokens, R currently unquantized tokens, D scalar channels per token, low-bit payload β, full precision f, and metadata cost A for completed groups:

Bbits=(S−R)Dβ+RDf+A,βeffective=β+RS(f−β)+ASD.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{bits}}&=(S-R)D\beta+RDf+A,\\\beta_{\mathrm{effective}}&=\beta+\frac RS(f-\beta)+\frac A{SD}.\end{aligned}Bbits​βeffective​​=(S−R)Dβ+RDf+A,=β+SR​(f−β)+SDA​.​

Here R is the actual retained residual length, which may vary with group flushing. The K and V grouping axes can give different A. As S becomes large, the residual fraction shrinks; on a short context it can dominate. The same nominal two-bit method can therefore have different effective bits at 2K and 128K context. Dequantization arithmetic, packed-layout support, scale loads, and the size of the extra kernels determine whether storage savings become latency savings.

Derivation: why the grouping axis changes weighted value error

For a fixed attention vector α and one output channel, quantized values contribute δo=Σi αi εi. The exact second moment is:

E[(δo)2]=(∑iαiE[εi])2+∑i∑jαiαjCov⁡(εi,εj).\mathbb E[(\delta o)^2]=\left(\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i]\right)^2+\sum_i\sum_j\alpha_i\alpha_j\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j).E[(δo)2]=(i∑​αi​E[εi​])2+i∑​j∑​αi​αj​Cov(εi​,εj​).

If errors are zero-mean and independent across tokens, this reduces to Σi αi²σi². If α is uniform over m tokens and variances equal σ², the result is σ²/m. If one token receives all attention, it is σ². The effective number of contributing tokens is therefore 1/Σiαi² under these assumptions; sequence length by itself does not control error averaging.

A quantization scale shared across tokens couples their error magnitudes and can introduce covariance or bias. A large value at an irrelevant token can enlarge the step used for a highly attended token. Per-token grouping restricts that range coupling, which can protect the weighted output even when its unweighted tensor MSE is not the smallest. This motivates KIVI's analysis rather than deriving its empirical performance from an independence assumption that real rounding need not satisfy.

For keys, the consumer is the dot product si=Σc qc ki,c/√d. Under independent zero-mean coordinate errors, Var(δsi)=Σc qc²σi,c²/d. A single large channel that sets a per-token scale can increase many σi,c values simultaneously. Per-channel scales can isolate that channel's range across a group of tokens. However, the desired allocation is weighted by qc², so a future-query-independent key MSE optimum need not be the attention-score optimum. This is the mathematical gap addressed by sensitivity-aware calibration, query-aware retrieval and task evaluation.

Exercise — Concentration changes the same quantizer’s error

Four independent zero-mean value errors each have variance 0.01. Compare output-error variance for α=(1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) and α=(0.7,0.1,0.1,0.1).

Show worked solution

Uniform attention gives 0.01·4·(1/4)²=0.0025. Concentrated attention gives 0.01·(0.49+0.01+0.01+0.01)=0.0052. Their effective token counts are 4 and 1/0.52≈1.923. The result depends on zero mean and independence; shared clipping bias or correlated errors can prevent this variance reduction.

5.3 KVQuant: pre-RoPE keys, calibrated codebooks, and sparse outliers

KVQuant also distinguishes key channels from value tokens, but takes a different route through the streaming problem. It calibrates key scales and thresholds offline, uses pre-RoPE key quantization to preserve stable channel structure, learns sensitivity-weighted nonuniform codebooks, and stores selected outliers separately in higher precision. Value statistics are computed at runtime because token magnitudes vary. The first token can be protected because sink-token error is disproportionately consequential. [16]

RoPE rotates channel pairs by position-dependent angles. A channel that was consistently large before rotation can distribute its magnitude differently after rotation. KVQuant quantizes the cleaner pre-rotation representation, then fuses dequantization and the required positional rotation into attention. This is a kernel contract: handing those pre-RoPE bytes to an attention kernel that expects already-rotated keys gives the wrong logits.

The nonuniform codebook uses a sensitivity-weighted objective of the form Σi Fii(ai−Q(ai))², with diagonal Fisher information estimated on calibration data. Codebook entries are shared at a coarse tensor/layer level and rescaled at the appropriate vector granularity. Dense-and-sparse quantization removes values that would otherwise set an excessive range, using per-vector thresholds rather than a single threshold for an entire layer. Indices for sparse exceptions consume bits too. Calibration makes runtime easier but introduces a distribution-shift question that KIVI’s online grouping treats differently.

For N dense slots, J stored exceptions, exception-value width f, index width j, scales A and codebook C, a layout that keeps all dense slots and adds an exception stream has:

Bbits=Nβ+J(f+j)+A+C+Bpadding,βeffective=β+JN(f+j)+A+C+BpaddingN.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{bits}}&=N\beta+J(f+j)+A+C+B_{\mathrm{padding}},\\\beta_{\mathrm{effective}}&=\beta+\frac JN(f+j)+\frac{A+C+B_{\mathrm{padding}}}{N}.\end{aligned}Bbits​βeffective​​=Nβ+J(f+j)+A+C+Bpadding​,=β+NJ​(f+j)+NA+C+Bpadding​​.​

If the representation removes exception slots or encodes deltas, its accounting changes. The formula must describe the actual format, not an ideal sparse tensor that the kernel never stores. KVQuant’s title about ten-million-token inference concerns memory feasibility under specified configurations; it does not establish that an ordinary checkpoint understands ten-million-token dependencies or that such inference meets an interactive latency target.

5.4 A controlled quality comparison, including the missing bits

The following rows come from the same KVQuant paper’s revised Table 3, using LLaMA-2-7B-32K on LongBench. Average bits were estimated at the reported average 12.2K context. These are useful within-paper comparisons, not independently reproduced measurements. Higher LongBench average is better. [16]

ConfigurationReported average bits per scalarLongBench averageDifference from FP16
FP161631.96reference
KIVI-2, group 32, residual 1283.1730.04−1.92 points
KVQuant-3bit with 1% outliers3.3331.21−0.75 points

The nominal two-bit KIVI and nominal three-bit KVQuant configurations have similar encoded averages in this setting. Comparing “2 versus 3 bits” would obscure the storage actually bought. In the same source’s RULER Table 4, FP16 averages 56.40, KIVI-2 averages 39.78, KVQuant-3bit-1% averages 53.65, and KVQuant-2bit-1% averages 36.54, at up to 32K context. The harder synthetic suite exposes losses that a small aggregate LongBench change can conceal. KIVI’s own paper reports strong results in its settings; model, evaluation protocol, residual policy, and effective budget must travel with the claim.

This table provides a reason to prefer the three-bit KVQuant configuration for these particular quality constraints. It does not settle latency, calibration convenience, new model compatibility, or a different implementation’s quality. A deployment should compare its supported kernels at equal actual memory budgets, then measure both downstream quality and service latency.

5.5 TurboQuant: make the distribution easier before coding it

TurboQuant’s 2025 preprint studies online vector quantization through geometric distortion. Normalize a vector, apply a random orthogonal rotation, and quantize each rotated coordinate using a scalar codebook optimized for the resulting coordinate distribution. For a uniformly rotated unit vector in d dimensions, a coordinate has density proportional to (1−x²)^((d−3)/2) on [−1,1], approximately Gaussian with variance 1/d at large d. This supports reusable Lloyd–Max codebooks rather than a separate codebook fitted to every incoming cache vector. [29]

u=x∥x∥,y=Πu,ΠTΠ=I,ij=nearest_codepoint⁡(yj),x^=∥x∥ ΠTcodebook⁡[i].\begin{aligned}u&=\frac{x}{\lVert x\rVert},&y&=\Pi u,&\Pi^{\mathsf T}\Pi&=I,\\i_j&=\operatorname{nearest\_codepoint}(y_j),\\\widehat x&=\lVert x\rVert\,\Pi^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{codebook}[\boldsymbol i].\end{aligned}uij​x​=∥x∥x​,=nearest_codepoint(yj​),=∥x∥ΠTcodebook[i].​y=Πu,ΠTΠ=I,

An orthogonal rotation preserves exact dot products if applied consistently to queries and keys. Quantization after rotation is approximate. MSE-optimal reconstruction is also not necessarily an unbiased estimator of the query–key inner product. TurboQuant’s inner-product variant spends b−1 bits per coordinate on the MSE approximation and one bit on a Quantized Johnson–Lindenstrauss (QJL) sketch of its residual r. With a Gaussian projection S and z=sign(Sr), a residual estimate is proportional to ∥r∥Sᵀz. Its expectation recovers the residual inner product under the stated randomization assumptions. Algorithm 2 additionally stores the residual norm.

The unbiasedness guarantee applies to an inner-product estimator. Softmax is nonlinear, so an unbiased logit estimate does not imply unbiased attention probabilities, identical sampled text, or zero task-quality loss. Random-rotation theory also should not be silently transferred to any deterministic Hadamard transform; practical structured transforms can approximate the desired behavior at much lower cost, but their distribution and kernel implementation need evaluation.

Accounting audit. The archived paper’s Section 4.3 labels a mixed-channel configuration “2.5-bit” and illustrates it with (32×3+96×2)/128. That expression equals 2.25, so the prose example contains an arithmetic inconsistency. Retain the authors’ nominal labels when discussing their results, but do not use that equation as a verified storage measurement. The general payload average is Σg Ngβg/Σg Ng; vector norms, residual norms, codebooks, channel indices, padding, and protected regions then add overhead. This is an example of why even primary-paper arithmetic deserves checking. [29]

5.6 UltraQuant: a kernel-friendly format changes the frontier

UltraQuant, a June 2026 preprint, separates a codebook-based quality reference from a hardware-native FP4 path. It uses rotation to improve the distribution, then encodes groups of 32 channels as FP4 E2M1 with an eight-bit UE8M0 scale. The group is 17 bytes, or 4.25 bits per scalar before alignment and protected layers. Queries use an FP8 path, and AMD CDNA4 scaled matrix instructions consume the FP4 operands and exponent scales directly. Avoiding repeated codebook gathers and explicit BF16 reconstruction is a central systems choice. [30]

The FP4 grid is fixed, so the scale controls how the rotated distribution fits it. The paper optimizes one constant c, uses group absmax m, and rounds log₂(cm) to obtain the stored power-of-two scale exponent. Its reported c=0.156 is an empirical fitted choice transferred across the evaluated model families, not a mathematical universal constant. The evaluated compressed configurations protect the first and last two attention layers with BF16 KV. If protected layers contain fraction f of all cached scalars, the idealized average is 4.25(1−f)+16f before other metadata—not 4.25 throughout the model.

The results illustrate why capacity and kernel speed need a joint evaluation. On the paper’s Gutenberg multi-turn MiniMax-M2.5 workload, TP=2 on MI355X and concurrency 32, UltraQuant reports 1.63× output throughput and 2.3× overall P50 TTFT improvement over FP8 KV. The late rounds improve TTFT 3.47× as the FP8 cache suffers residency pressure, while the early warm rounds favor FP8 (reported ratio 0.86×). A single headline would hide this crossover. [30]

Quality is close in some settings and measurably worse in others. On its fixed 100-task SWE-bench Lite cohort, MiniMax resolves 62 tasks with BF16 or FP8 and 59 with UltraQuant; Qwen3-235B resolves 28 with BF16, 21 with FP8, and 24 with UltraQuant. These small cohorts do not establish a universal ranking or statistical equivalence. They show that bit width alone does not order task quality, and “near baseline” must not be rewritten as “lossless.” The paper is a recent preprint; these are reported results with a specific hardware and software path. [30]

6 · A codec for moving KV is a different object from an attention format

6.1 CacheGen: exploit locality, then adapt to the network

CacheGen targets loading precomputed context across a constrained or changing link. It groups nearby tokens, stores an anchor, and encodes each other token’s KV difference from that anchor. Correlated tensors give delta symbols a more concentrated distribution. Layer-dependent quantization assigns different error budgets, and channel/layer-specific entropy models drive arithmetic coding. The quantization is lossy; the subsequent entropy coder is lossless relative to those quantized symbols. [17]

All deltas in a group reference the same anchor. This allows parallel reconstruction rather than a dependency chain where decoding token i requires first decoding every earlier token. The original design uses ten-token groups and relatively higher precision for the anchor because its error affects the reconstructed group. Anchor choice, group length, and error budgets can vary, but changing them changes both compression and random-access behavior.

CacheGen pre-encodes context chunks at several quality levels. While fetching a context, it can choose another encoded level or transmit text and recompute the remaining chunk if available bandwidth changes. The decision is not simply “always send the smallest cache.” Encoding/decoding time, remaining SLO, quality, compute availability, and transmission overlap all matter. A useful simplified criterion is:

Tload=Tlookup+BencodedBWeffective+Tdecode+Tlayout,Trecompute=Tcompute queue+Tprefill(prefix),Tload<Trecompute(reuse, subject to quality).\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{load}}&=T_{\mathrm{lookup}}+\frac{B_{\mathrm{encoded}}}{\mathrm{BW}_{\mathrm{effective}}}+T_{\mathrm{decode}}+T_{\mathrm{layout}},\\T_{\mathrm{recompute}}&=T_{\mathrm{compute\ queue}}+T_{\mathrm{prefill}}(\text{prefix}),\\T_{\mathrm{load}}&<T_{\mathrm{recompute}}\qquad\text{(reuse, subject to quality).}\end{aligned}Tload​Trecompute​Tload​​=Tlookup​+BWeffective​Bencoded​​+Tdecode​+Tlayout​,=Tcompute queue​+Tprefill​(prefix),<Trecompute​(reuse, subject to quality).​

An entropy-coded bitstream generally cannot be fed directly into a GPU attention kernel expecting fixed-size random-access pages. It first needs decoding and possibly conversion to the engine’s storage layout. Thus a sixfold transfer compression ratio does not necessarily imply a sixfold resident KV reduction. Separate the representation on disk, on the wire, in host staging, and in the attention kernel.

6.2 CacheBlend: cached chunks need contextual repair

Suppose document B was cached independently and is later placed after document A. RoPE correction can adjust B’s positions, but its deeper hidden states also depend on attention to A. Correcting positions alone cannot reconstruct those states. Full recomputation is exact but expensive; naive concatenation is fast but omits cross-chunk interactions. CacheBlend recomputes selected token states to repair the most consequential discrepancies. [18]

At a layer, selected query rows attend to both reused and updated KV, and their states progress through the layer to generate repaired KV for subsequent layers. The paper observes that a minority of tokens have high KV deviation and that their ranks correlate across adjacent layers. Its practical selection starts with broad recomputation early, then progressively filters candidates using observed deviations, avoiding the impossible requirement of knowing the fully recomputed deep-layer cache in advance.

The reported 10–20% recomputation fractions are empirical operating points, not an exactness theorem. Repair quality depends on inter-document dependencies, prompt composition, model and depth. A task comparing contradictory statements across chunks may need interactions absent from a simple retrieval question. CacheBlend also pipelines loading with computation; end-to-end gain depends on whether the avoided compute was actually on the critical path. This method changes the admissible reuse relation: exact prefix reuse remains exact, whereas non-prefix chunk fusion becomes an explicitly approximate operation.

Derivation: positional correction cannot repair changed causal content

A two-token, two-layer toy transformer is enough to demonstrate the problem. Ignore positions, use scalar values, and set all first-layer attention logits to zero. Then causal softmax is uniform over available tokens. Let the residual update be hi′=hi+attentioni, with identity value projection and no FFN. Token A has embedding a and token B has embedding b.

B alone:hB′=b+b=2b,B after A:hB′=b+a+b2=a+3b2,Difference=a+3b2−2b=a−b2.\begin{aligned}\text{$B$ alone:}\quad h'_B&=b+b=2b,\\\text{$B$ after $A$:}\quad h'_B&=b+\frac{a+b}{2}=\frac{a+3b}{2},\\\text{Difference}&=\frac{a+3b}{2}-2b=\frac{a-b}{2}.\end{aligned}B alone:hB′​B after A:hB′​Difference​=b+b=2b,=b+2a+b​=2a+3b​,=2a+3b​−2b=2a−b​.​

If layer two's key projection is identity, its cached key for B differs by (a−b)/2. There are no positional embeddings in this counterexample, so no position offset could repair it. With RoPE, correcting position solves an additional rotation mismatch but leaves the changed hidden-state content.

This also explains the depth dependence of repair. The first layer's input projection for B can be computed from its unchanged embedding, while later-layer KV depends on the newly contextualized state. Selectively recomputing B's query/output changes the hidden state fed into the next layer; simply replacing a later key without recomputing its causal ancestors is a different approximation.

CacheBlend's observed sparsity of high-deviation tokens creates an opportunity to approximate this repair cheaply. The counterexample shows why repair is needed, not why a fixed 10% fraction must suffice. For dense cross-document dependencies, many tokens can change. A mathematical guarantee would require bounds on cross-chunk attention, value magnitudes and propagation through subsequent layers, which are stronger assumptions than “the chunks contain the same text.”

Exercise — Compute the invalid cached key

In the toy model let a=6 and b=2. What is B’s cached layer-two key alone and after A? What happens if a=b instead?

Show worked solution

Alone it is 2b=4; after A it is (6+3·2)/2=6. The key error is 2. If a=b, this particular toy difference vanishes, showing why a benign example can make arbitrary chunk stitching appear exact. One counterexample suffices to disprove a general exactness claim; one equality example cannot establish it.

7 · 2023–2024: when KV moves out of HBM

7.1 FlexGen: amortize transfers with an execution schedule

FlexGen studies high-throughput inference when model state exceeds one GPU’s capacity, using GPU, CPU memory, and disk. It chooses placements for weights, activations and KV and schedules computation to reuse transferred data across microbatches. A weight block loaded once and used on many sequences can be much cheaper than repeatedly fetching it for small independent requests. Its optimization formulation exposes capacity and bandwidth constraints rather than treating offload as a single on/off flag. [8]

The two diagrams traverse the same layer–token–batch computation grid in different orders. Row-by-row execution follows individual microbatches through many layers. The block schedule groups work so a transferred layer’s weights serve more examples before being displaced. That amortization explains high token throughput even when an individual sequence waits much longer. FlexGen’s prominent OPT-175B-on-a-16GB-GPU result is a feasibility and throughput result under offloading and batching, not evidence of low interactive latency for every request.

This distinction is fundamental to memory hierarchies. Weight bytes can be amortized across B tokens in a batch; KV bytes for independent sequences remain largely sequence-specific. If offload transfers the entire historical KV every decode step, longer contexts eventually make the link the bottleneck even if weights are perfectly reused. Compression, selection, or moving attention computation toward the cache can address that remaining cost.

7.2 InfiniGen: predict useful host KV before the next layer

InfiniGen retains a larger history in host memory and prefetches the entries likely to matter for the next attention layer. This avoids permanently discarding history while reducing CPU–GPU traffic. Its predictor uses the empirical similarity of adjacent layers’ attention inputs, plus a small subset of important query/key dimensions. [9]

The offline transformation multiplies Q and K by the same orthogonal matrix A. Algebraically, (QA)(KA)ᵀ=QAAᵀKᵀ=QKᵀ. An SVD-derived basis concentrates query energy into fewer dimensions. During prefill, the method chooses influential columns from the transformed query/key statistics; the paper uses 30% of columns in its studied configuration. During decode, the previous layer’s available input approximates the next layer’s query, scores partial keys, and selects candidates before the real next-layer query is ready.

The timeline shows where the overlap comes from. Selection for layer i occurs while executing layer i−1. Host transfers can run during intervening attention/FFN work. A threshold relative to the largest predicted logit selects entries: score > max(score)−a. After softmax, a logit difference a corresponds to an individual weight ratio exp(−a), but many individually small omitted terms can still have meaningful total mass. The criterion is an approximation; the orthogonal transformation’s exact algebra does not make the predictor exact.

RoPE and other position-dependent operations must remain consistent with any transformed basis. The paper’s equality concerns the transformed query/key operands used in its design; arbitrary insertion of an orthogonal matrix before an incompatible rotation is not justified by AAᵀ=I. Host memory is also finite, so InfiniGen includes pool management under pressure. It extends the recoverable horizon relative to aggressive GPU eviction, but a later host eviction can still remove history.

7.3 FastDecode: move the operation to the state

FastDecode takes another direction: sequence-specific attention executes on CPU workers holding their KV, while GPU workers handle operations whose shared model weights benefit from batching. It transfers queries and resulting activations instead of repeatedly moving the entire historical cache. In the paper’s terminology these are R-workers for sequence-related computation and S-workers for shared-weight computation. [26]

A rough layer comparison explains the opportunity. Moving dense KV costs O(SHkv d) bytes; sending query/output activations costs O(Hq d), though multiple transfers and synchronization are needed. CPU attention still scans the history using CPU memory bandwidth and compute. The service must have enough CPU bandwidth and well-balanced workers to keep the GPU occupied. The bottom panel shows how unequal sequence lengths and stage times create idle gaps despite an apparently balanced average.

This is a compute-placement system, not simply a cache spilled to DDR. It is attractive when the avoided transfer and GPU capacity gains outweigh CPU attention latency, network traffic, scheduling overhead and additional servers. Comparing only the GPU count can conceal CPU cost and energy. It also demonstrates a general design choice: either bring data to computation, bring computation to data, or reduce the necessary information before moving it.

8 · 2024–2026: a shared KV service across the memory hierarchy

8.1 Mooncake: disaggregate phases around the state pool

Mooncake separates prefill and decode and organizes a distributed KV pool using CPU memory and other storage resources. Prefill prioritizes efficient creation/reuse of state and TTFT; decode prioritizes token cadence and sustained throughput. A cache-centric scheduler coordinates prefix locality, load, available capacity and transfer cost. The architecture makes KV placement a first-class scheduling decision. [19]

The figure contains three interacting pools: prefill instances, cache capacity, and decode instances. Allocating more decoders does not help if prefill cannot feed them or cache transfer saturates the fabric. Maximizing local prefix reuse does not help if it sends all work to one overloaded prefill instance. The objectives written beside the diagram explicitly contain both latency and capacity constraints.

Follow s1 through s4. A prefiller loads reusable prefix state, computes the new suffix, and makes the resulting state available to a decoder. Layerwise load/store can overlap with computation where dependencies permit; the decoder loads the state before consuming it. A transfer is not free just because RDMA avoids an extra CPU copy. NIC bandwidth, PCIe paths, registration, synchronization, memory layout and shared-fabric congestion still determine when the consuming kernel can start.

Mooncake’s block hashes include preceding-prefix identity, allowing deduplication without confusing equal local token blocks under different contexts. Its reported large throughput gains combine scheduling, reuse, phase separation and workloads with substantial reusable context. The paper includes both simulations and production-related traces; they should not be collapsed into one universal GPU speedup. In the archived evaluation, the request trace’s mean input and output lengths are 7,590 and 182 tokens. This strongly shapes the balance between prefill savings and decode capacity. [19]

8.2 LMCache: standardize lifecycle and movement across engines

LMCache provides a cache layer between inference engines and heterogeneous memory/storage backends. Its engine connector handles layout and lifecycle integration, while the cache engine, token processor, event manager, storage manager, allocator and transfer channels carry different responsibilities. The same infrastructure can support reusable-context caching, cross-engine movement, and prefill/decode disaggregation. [20]

Reading the boxes matters. A remote backend determines where bytes can be stored; it does not by itself decide which request should run next. The token processor identifies compatible cached regions. Events represent asynchronous operations whose completion must be respected. The connector translates between an engine’s cache layout and the external layer. A backend hit can therefore incur several costs before it becomes an attention-ready tensor.

Fine-grained engine pages are not automatically efficient network messages. The paper contrasts small transfers with aggregated chunks and overlaps layerwise KV loading with computation. Large chunks improve bandwidth utilization and reduce per-operation overhead, while small chunks improve reuse granularity and avoid fetching unused tails. Storage chunk size, attention page size and scheduling unit can be different; forcing them all to one size gives up design freedom.

In its single-node CPU-offload evaluation, LMCache uses an H100 server, model-dependent GPU allocations, up to 500 GB of host cache, and multi-round document QA with approximately 10K input tokens (20K for Llama-3.1-8B) and at most 100 output tokens. It reports 1.9–8.1× lower TTFT at low QPS and 2.3–14× higher query throughput at matched TTFT across evaluated models. Baselines and versions differ by configuration; the paper identifies LMCache v0.3.6, vLLM v0.10.2 for the base engine and v0.11.0 for its CPU-offload comparison. These are reuse-heavy service results, not a claim that moving one cold prefix through host RAM is always faster than computing it. [20]

8.3 The NVIDIA hierarchy the original question alluded to

NVIDIA’s March 2026 CMX description names G1 as GPU HBM, G2 as system RAM, G3 as local SSD, and G4 as shared storage. It introduces a G3.5 tier of Ethernet-attached flash using BlueField-4, intended for pooled reusable context and prestaging toward compute. The advertised “up to 5×” TPS/power-efficiency improvements are vendor system claims, not a general flash-versus-HBM benchmark. [22]

Its April 2026 Dynamo material connects agent lifecycle hints, KV-aware routing, and retention to the serving engine. NIXL supplies transfer mechanisms across supported memory/storage paths; it is not, by itself, an eviction or semantic cache-validity policy. [23] [24]

The following engineering interpretation applies beyond one vendor’s tier names. Active dense attention needs high sustained bandwidth. Paused prefixes need predictable restoration before reuse. Cold derived state can tolerate higher access latency if recomputation is even more expensive. Flash expands economical capacity; it does not acquire HBM bandwidth merely because a framework exposes it behind a common API. Persistent application records and recomputable KV also need different durability decisions.

LocationUseful roleDominant performance questionsCommon mistake
GPU HBM / local accelerator memoryActive attention state and immediate reuseCapacity, bandwidth, page layout, concurrent kernelsCounting weights alone when sizing a server
Host DDR or coherent system memoryPaused state, staging, CPU attention, spillNUMA placement, link path, pinned buffers, overlapTreating all host bytes as reachable at headline bandwidth
