8.4 Transfer versus recomputation: work the numbers

Consider the 16 GiB cache from Section 1. At a measured effective 25 GB/s path, a complete one-way transfer takes at least 16×2³⁰/(25×10⁹)=0.687 seconds. At 7 GB/s it takes about 2.45 seconds. These are illustrative bandwidth assumptions, not specifications for a named device; queueing, conversion and synchronization add time. If recomputing that prefix takes 900 ms on an otherwise available GPU, the first link might make restoration worthwhile, while the second does not unless another benefit or overlap changes the critical path.

Now ask whether this is one restore or a read every token. A 687 ms one-time restore can amortize over many subsequent tokens. Repeating it for each token caps throughput below 1.5 tokens/s before any model computation. A capacity design suitable for paused sessions can therefore be unsuitable for active dense decode. Selection, compression or CPU attention changes the transferred quantity and must be accounted for explicitly.

For a prefix with probability p of reuse during its retained lifetime, a rough retention value is p·max(0,Trecompute−Trestore), divided by bytes and residence time if capacity is priced that way. This gives a reason to retain an expensive, moderately popular long prefix over a cheap frequently used short one. It is only a heuristic: concurrent demand, shared ancestors, compute congestion and future eviction interactions make the full problem dynamic. Admission and replacement should use measured distributions rather than a single average hit ratio.

Derivation: layerwise restoration is a scheduling recurrence

Suppose a prefix has L layer segments. Segment ℓ takes transfer time tℓ on one copy engine and compute time cℓ once that layer can run on the GPU. Transfers are issued sequentially in layer order, and compute layers are sequential; the two engines can overlap. Let Aℓ be transfer completion and Fℓ compute completion, with A0=F0=0.

Aℓ=Aℓ−1+tℓ,Fℓ=max⁡(Aℓ,Fℓ−1)+cℓ.\begin{aligned}A_\ell&=A_{\ell-1}+t_\ell,\\F_\ell&=\max(A_\ell,F_{\ell-1})+c_\ell.\end{aligned}Aℓ​Fℓ​​=Aℓ−1​+tℓ​,=max(Aℓ​,Fℓ−1​)+cℓ​.​

Layer ℓ waits for both its bytes and the preceding layer's output. This recurrence is more informative than subtracting total transfer from total compute. With uniform t and c, induction gives FL=t+c+(L−1)max(t,c). If t≤c, transfers after the first can be hidden in this ideal pipeline; if t>c, every later layer exposes t−c additional stall. Startup and drain remain even in perfect steady state.

Real overlap can fail if copies and kernels share a saturated HBM path, if layout conversion must occur on the GPU, or if an early missing page blocks a whole layer. Transfer completion also needs memory ownership and lifetime guarantees. The recurrence assumes data can be prefetched before its consuming query is computed; a query-dependent retrieval policy may reveal its selected addresses too late to achieve this overlap.

A restore-versus-recompute decision should compare actual completion times under the same resource queues. A 200 ms restore is attractive against 300 ms isolated prefill only if the copy path is sufficiently available and restore does not displace more valuable live state. If recomputation can overlap other transfers or reuse already resident lower layers, its critical path changes too. “Bytes divided by bandwidth” is a component lower bound, not the whole service latency.

Exercise — Two orderings with the same total bytes

For three layers, transfers take (1,8,1) ms and compute takes (5,5,5) ms. Compute F3. Compare with transfer times (8,1,1), which have the same sum.

Show worked solution

For (1,8,1), A=(1,9,10). F1=max(1,0)+5=6; F2=max(9,6)+5=14; F3=max(10,14)+5=19 ms. For (8,1,1), A=(8,9,10) and F=(13,18,23) ms. Equal bytes and total transfer time give different latency because putting the long transfer first delays pipeline startup. This does not authorize arbitrary layer reordering—the model's dependency order remains fixed.

9 · The research lineage: landmarks and the questions their variants answer

The dates below follow first reports where possible; a later conference date does not move a method’s first appearance. Parallel branches overlap. Architectural sharing, virtual memory, precision, sparsity, reuse and tiering can coexist in one system.

Period / landmarkCore bottleneckMechanism and associated variantsWhat the next generation had to solve
2019 MQA → 2023 GQA → 2024 MLAToo many cached scalar dimensionsShare KV heads; interpolate head sharing; cache a latent plus positional branchPreserve quality and design kernels that realize the smaller representation
2023 FlexGenState exceeds GPU capacityPlacement and loop scheduling across GPU, RAM and diskInteractive latency and repeated KV-transfer cost

9.1 Choose by the measured bottleneck

Observed symptomFirst method family to investigateEvidence that would justify adopting it
GPU memory reserved but little useful KV presentPaged allocation or virtual-memory managementMore admitted requests at equal latency, fewer wasted bytes
Repeated long prompts dominate TTFTExact prefix reuse and locality-aware schedulingAvoided prefill time exceeds lookup, transfer and queueing costs
KV payload itself prevents the target concurrencyGQA/MLA model choice; supported KV quantizationActual allocated bytes fall while task quality and latency remain acceptable
Long-context attention dominates decode latencyQuest-like retrieval, optimized low-bit attentionEnd-to-end gain after scoring, top-k, conversion and dense-layer costs
A fixed window loses important distant evidenceLarger retained state, query-aware retrieval, or host-backed recoveryMulti-hop, changing-question and late-recall evaluations recover quality
Paused agent sessions evict each otherHost/flash tiering with lifecycle-aware retentionFewer re-prefills and better late-round TTFT on realistic arrival traces
PCIe traffic dominates every tokenInfiniGen-style selective prefetch or FastDecode-style placementLower critical-path transfer without excessive quality or CPU cost
Separate documents are reused in different combinationsCacheBlend-like repair or full recomputationCross-document answer quality at a measured recomputation fraction

These are diagnoses, not a global ranking. A paged FP8 GQA cache with host prefix offload is a coherent combination because the components address different costs. Combining permanent eviction with a policy that promises arbitrary future retrieval is more delicate: the latter cannot recover data the former destroyed. The location of a full backing copy determines whether “evicted” means unavailable on the GPU or unavailable everywhere.

Derivation: a prefix’s cache value depends on reuse time and saved work

Consider a simplified retention problem. Prefix i consumes Mi bytes. Future requests that can reuse it arrive as a Poisson process with rate λi, so the waiting time T to the next reuse has P(T>t)=exp(−λit). Assume only the first reuse during a chosen retention interval τ earns a benefit Δi=max(0,Trecompute−Trestore), measured in saved service time. Let memory rent be ρ service-time-equivalent units per byte per unit time, and keep the object for the full τ.

Expected benefit=ΔiPr⁡(T≤τ)=Δi(1−e−λiτ),Cost=ρMiτ,Ji(τ)=Δi(1−e−λiτ)−ρMiτ,Ji′(τ)=λiΔie−λiτ−ρMi,Ji′′(τ)=−λi2Δie−λiτ≤0.\begin{aligned}\text{Expected benefit}&=\Delta_i\Pr(T\le\tau)=\Delta_i(1-e^{-\lambda_i\tau}),\\\text{Cost}&=\rho M_i\tau,\\J_i(\tau)&=\Delta_i(1-e^{-\lambda_i\tau})-\rho M_i\tau,\\J_i'(\tau)&=\lambda_i\Delta_i e^{-\lambda_i\tau}-\rho M_i,\\J_i''(\tau)&=-\lambda_i^2\Delta_i e^{-\lambda_i\tau}\le0.\end{aligned}Expected benefitCostJi​(τ)Ji′​(τ)Ji′′​(τ)​=Δi​Pr(T≤τ)=Δi​(1−e−λi​τ),=ρMi​τ,=Δi​(1−e−λi​τ)−ρMi​τ,=λi​Δi​e−λi​τ−ρMi​,=−λi2​Δi​e−λi​τ≤0.​

Concavity makes the stationary point a global maximum. If λiΔi≤ρMi, the optimum is τ*=0. Otherwise τ*=log(λiΔi/(ρMi))/λi. Thus identical hit probabilities do not imply identical value: expensive-to-recompute prefixes can justify longer residence, while slow restore reduces the benefit.

This is a teaching model with a priced capacity constraint, not a claim that real arrivals are Poisson or that a TTL policy is optimal for all engines. Repeated hits, shared ancestors, eviction on first reuse, uncertain future return times, and multiple tiers change the objective. In particular, keeping one radix ancestor can support many descendants, so items are not independent. The derivation nevertheless identifies the quantities that a useful heuristic must estimate: reuse hazard, saved work, byte cost and residence time.

A tool pause supplies information about reuse timing. If the next use is likely just after a known tool deadline, a scheduled prefetch can dominate continuous HBM residence. Such a policy is valuable because it changes the conditional reuse distribution, not because TTL alone creates bandwidth.

9.2 A benchmark protocol that answers the right question

Start with the same model revision, tokenizer, prompt tokens, positional settings, output policy, and quality tasks. Report the actual cache representation, including K versus V precision, scales, residual length, outliers, protected layers, head sharing, page/chunk sizes and peak workspaces. Record hardware topology and effective link bandwidth; a remote host path and a coherent CPU–GPU path are not interchangeable.

Then replay workloads with arrival times, input/output lengths, shared-prefix distributions, tool-pause durations and concurrency. Measure P50/P95/P99 TTFT and ITL, SLO-qualified throughput, GPU/CPU memory, network and storage traffic, preemption/recompute counts, and cost per successful request. Include cold starts, warm prefixes and capacity-pressure phases separately. A cache can look excellent after a synthetic warmup and fail when the working set expands.

For approximate methods, quality needs several failure modes: multiple needles, aggregation over many facts, conflicting documents, questions unknown at compression time, long generated reasoning, code editing and multi-turn tasks. Perplexity, single-needle retrieval and task success test different behaviors. An average can hide catastrophic regressions on one critical task. Compare equal allocated memory or service cost, not equal nominal bit labels or selected-token counts when implementations use different metadata and GQA expansion.

Finally perform ablations that identify causality. Disable reuse while retaining the same kernel to isolate cache hits. Hold the batch fixed to separate a faster attention kernel from capacity-enabled larger batches. Measure quantization and data movement independently before interpreting the whole service. The goal is to learn which removed cost explains the gain and whether that cost exists in the intended deployment.

10 · Deeper deductions and a study route

State compression and compute compression are separate budgets. Quest can save reads without reducing full backing-store capacity. Prefix reuse can remove prefill while leaving decode untouched. KV quantization can improve concurrency without speeding an individual kernel. A rigorous design tracks bytes stored, bytes moved, FLOPs executed, and time on the dependency path as separate quantities.

More memory can make routing harder. A larger distributed cache creates more possible placements and stale availability information. If the scheduler cannot exploit locality without creating queues, extra capacity has little marginal value. Conversely, moderate compression can have a discontinuous benefit when it keeps a frequently reused working set resident. UltraQuant’s early-versus-late-round result illustrates such a threshold, not merely a uniform bandwidth multiplier.

A recoverable history and a compressed belief are different interfaces. A full host-backed history can answer a new retrieval query at additional transfer cost. A permanently pruned cache encodes a bet about future relevance. Applications should choose that bet deliberately: a streaming transcription model, a legal-document comparison task, and a coding agent revisiting earlier files have different information-retention requirements.

The emerging optimization unit is a request’s future lifetime. A tool pause makes immediate HBM residency unnecessary but can make later restoration valuable. An agent’s likely return time and output length provide information that pure token-level cache statistics lack. Research opportunities include joint scheduling of computation and restoration, calibrated future-reuse estimates, precision changes across tiers, and quality-aware admission for heterogeneous requests.

For a first close reading, derive Section 1’s memory count, then read PagedAttention’s allocation/share diagrams and SGLang’s radix operations. Next compare H2O, SnapKV and Quest using the question “can a previously unimportant token come back?” Read KIVI and KVQuant side by side to connect grouping axes to error propagation. Finish with CacheGen, Mooncake and LMCache to see how an algorithm becomes a service under transfer and queueing constraints. TurboQuant and UltraQuant then show the tension between geometric distortion, metadata, and a real low-bit matrix instruction.

Exercises with checkable conclusions

  • Paging: for sequence lengths 17, 32 and 33 with 16-token pages and no sharing, allocation is 32+32+48=112 token slots for 82 useful tokens. Tail waste is 30 slots. Changing to eight-token pages gives 24+32+40=96 slots and 14 wasted slots, before the extra page-table cost.
  • Mixed precision: if 28 of 32 equally sized layers use 4.25-bit KV and four use BF16, the scalar-weighted average is 5.71875 bits, before alignment and other metadata. Quoting four bits understates the stored state substantially.
  • Restore: a 4 GiB encoded prefix over an effective 25 GB/s path takes at least 171.8 ms one way. Add 15 ms decode/conversion and 20 ms queueing to get 206.8 ms. Compare this with measured prefix recomputation, not the full request’s unrelated latency.
  • Amdahl: if attention is 60% of baseline decode time, making it seven times faster yields 1/(0.4+0.6/7)=2.06× total speedup before new overhead. A sevenfold attention result cannot by itself justify sevenfold token throughput.
  • Reuse identity: independently cached B cannot generally be appended after A with exact deep-layer KV using a RoPE offset alone. Explain the missing causal dependency, then identify which approximation CacheBlend repairs.

References & reading route

Primary papers and official technical documents. Dates identify first reports or publication, not a claim of independent reproduction. Numerical results retain their original conditions.

  1. Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need. 2019. Multi-query attention reduces KV heads.
  2. GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints. 2023. Grouped-query architecture and uptraining.
  3. DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model. 2024. Multi-head latent attention and compressed cache representation.
  4. Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention. SOSP 2023. Block allocation, sharing, and vLLM.
  5. vAttention: Dynamic Memory Management for Serving LLMs without PagedAttention. 2024. Contiguous virtual addressing with dynamic physical pages.
  6. SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs. 2023/2024. RadixAttention and prefix reuse.
  7. Preble: Efficient Distributed Prompt Scheduling for LLM Serving. 2024. Cluster scheduling with prefix locality and load balance.
  8. FlexGen: High-Throughput Generative Inference of Large Language Models with a Single GPU. 2023. GPU/CPU/disk placement and throughput-oriented execution.
  9. InfiniGen: Efficient Generative Inference with Dynamic KV Cache Management. OSDI 2024. Predict and prefetch important KV entries from host memory.
  10. H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models. 2023. Attention-score-based retention plus recent tokens.
  11. Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks. 2023/2024. StreamingLLM: sink tokens and rolling recent window.
  12. SnapKV: LLM Knows What You are Looking for Before Generation. 2024. Observation-window-based prompt KV selection.
  13. PyramidKV: Dynamic KV Cache Compression based on Pyramidal Information Funneling. 2024/2025. Allocate different KV budgets across depth.
  14. Quest: Query-Aware Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference. 2024. Page min/max metadata and query-aware retrieval.
  15. KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache. 2024. Different grouping for keys and values; recent residual window.
  16. KVQuant: Towards 10 Million Context Length LLM Inference with KV Cache Quantization. 2024. Pre-RoPE keys, channel quantization, nonuniform formats, and outliers.
  17. CacheGen: KV Cache Compression and Streaming for Fast Large Language Model Serving. 2023/2024. Encoded transport with adaptive compression/recomputation.
  18. CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion. 2024. Selective recomputation when combining cached chunks.
  19. Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving. 2024. CPU/DRAM/SSD cache pool, scheduling, and phase separation.
  20. LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference. 2025. Cross-engine storage and data-movement layer.
  21. DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized LLM Serving. 2024. SLOs and prefill/decode resource allocation.
  22. NVIDIA BlueField-4-Powered CMX Context Memory Storage Platform. March 16, 2026. Official vendor account of G1–G4 and a G3.5 flash tier; claims are vendor-reported.
  23. Full-Stack Optimizations for Agentic Inference with NVIDIA Dynamo. April 17, 2026. Four-tier hierarchy, cache-aware routing, and lifecycle hints.
  24. NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library: distributed inference data movement. March 9, 2026. Official transfer-layer architecture.
  25. LongBench: A Bilingual, Multitask Benchmark for Long Context Understanding. 2023. Multiple tasks beyond single-needle retrieval.
  26. FastDecode: High-Throughput GPU-Efficient LLM Serving using Heterogeneous Pipelines. 2024. CPU attention workers and GPU shared-weight computation.
  27. Ada-KV: Optimizing KV Cache Eviction by Adaptive Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Inference. 2024 preprint / NeurIPS 2025. Head budgets from retained attention mass.
  28. Not All Heads Matter: A Head-Level KV Cache Compression Method with Integrated Retrieval and Reasoning. 2024 preprint / ICLR 2025. HeadKV-R and HeadKV-R2.
  29. TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate. 2025 preprint / ICLR 2026. Random rotation, scalar codebooks, residual QJL correction.
  30. UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents. June 2026 preprint. Hardware-native FP4 KV on AMD GPUs; quality and serving tradeoffs.
